_description: Single source of truth for the app: the case-level session schema (forum/jurisdiction lives here, asked once) plus the index of every issue file in content/issues/.

forum.prompt: Is this motion being filed in state or federal court?
forum.asked: once, at the very start of the wizard, before any issue-taxonomy questions — every issue's law_paragraph rendering reads this instead of asking again
forum.note: Replaces the old 3-option jurisdiction_selection (Federal only / State only / Federal and state). SCOTUS authority binds state courts too, so a state-court filing always includes SCOTUS + the selected state together — there is no 'state only, no SCOTUS' option anymore.

state_name.asked: once, only if forum is 'State court'
state_name.note: Currently only one option, matching this project's present scope. Its value maps to the court code 'AK' used throughout segments and authorities. Expanding to a new state later means adding a dropdown option here and a new court value (e.g. 'CA') in the affected issue files — no other structural change.

federal_circuit.asked: once, only if forum is 'Federal court'
federal_circuit.note: Currently only one option, matching this project's present scope. Its value is used directly as the court code. Expanding to a new circuit later means adding a dropdown option here and using its name as a new court value in the affected issue files.

case_session_schema.answers: object — keyed by question id, populated as the attorney moves through each issue's trigger.questions
case_session_schema.matched_issues: array of issue ids — populated by matching logic, not asked directly

circuits_reviewed_field.location: top level of each issue file, e.g. issue.circuits_reviewed
circuits_reviewed_field.format: array of court values (from federal_circuit) that have actually been checked for their OWN case law on this issue, e.g. ['9th Circuit'] — a circuit CAN be in this list with no circuit-specific segment authored, meaning 'checked, nothing beyond the SCOTUS segment worth citing'
circuits_reviewed_field.why_separate_from_segments: Without this, the resolver can't distinguish 'checked, nothing circuit-specific to add' from 'nobody has looked yet' — both look identical (no circuit-specific segment) unless tracked explicitly.
circuits_reviewed_field.current_scope: Only ever contains '9th Circuit' for now, since that's the only circuit in scope — see case_session_schema.federal_circuit.

review_condition_rendering.description: Separate from resolveLawParagraph. After an issue is matched (or considered) and its law_paragraph text is rendered, check the issue's review_conditions: for each one whose 'when' evaluates true against case_session.answers, append its display_note to the output.
review_condition_rendering.format: Append on its own line after the law paragraph text, wrapped as: [NOTE: <display_note>] — all-caps 'NOTE' and brackets so it's visually distinct from the drafted law text when the attorney reviews the output.
review_condition_rendering.why_separate_from_flag: 'flag' is a short machine-readable id (for logging/analytics — e.g. tracking how often intent_below_franks_standard fires across cases). 'display_note' is the attorney-facing sentence that actually explains the judgment call. Never surface 'flag' itself in the output — it's not written for a human reader.

excluded_explanations_rendering.description: For issues whose match_condition did NOT pass, check excluded_explanations: if any entry's 'when' evaluates true against case_session.answers, the issue was a close call worth explaining, even though it isn't included in the motion.
steps: 1. For every issue considered (not just matched ones), if match_condition failed, check its excluded_explanations list.
2. Collect { issue_label, display_note } for each entry whose 'when' evaluates true.

3. If any were collected, render them together in ONE section at the very end of the full document — after all matched issues' law paragraphs/notes, and after cross_cutting_reminders — e.g. under a heading like 'Issues Considered But Not Included'.
4. If nothing was collected, omit the section entirely — don't show an empty heading.
excluded_explanations_rendering.why_separate_from_review_conditions: review_conditions flags a shaky INCLUDED issue, rendered inline with that issue's law paragraph. excluded_explanations explains a NOT-included issue, rendered once at the end since there's no law paragraph to attach it to — the issue never made it into the motion body at all.
excluded_explanations_rendering.why_not_every_failed_match_gets_one: Most excluded issues fail match_condition simply because the fact pattern doesn't exist for this case (e.g. no warrant was used at all) — that's not a close call and needs no explanation. excluded_explanations only fires for the specific, legally meaningful near-misses you've deliberately documented, not every unmatched issue.

cross_cutting_reminders.description: Standing and fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree/attenuation aren't triggered by a specific fact pattern the way most issues are — they apply to EVERY suppression issue, always. Rather than referencing them per-issue (which doesn't scale and is easy to forget on any given issue file), render a single reminder once per motion, whenever at least one issue matched — not once per matched issue.

reminders.display_note: Before relying on any issue above, confirm the defendant has standing to challenge it — i.e., a reasonable expectation of privacy in the place or thing searched. Standing is assessed separately for each matched issue; having it for one doesn't establish it for another.

For each matched issue, consider whether the evidence you're seeking to suppress is a direct or derivative product of that violation, versus sufficiently attenuated to survive suppression even if the underlying issue is found.

cross_cutting_reminders.rendering: Render once at the end of the motion's full output (after every matched issue's law paragraph and notes), not repeated per issue.

authority_schema.description: Every legal authority cited in a segment's law_paragraph text lives in ONE unified 'authorities' array. Each entry carries a 'type' (case/statute/constitution/rule) and a single 'court' field — the SAME field and value space as segment.court (see court_tagging_convention) — rather than a separate 'jurisdiction' field.

shape.name: the case name, or the statute/rule/constitutional provision identifier
shape.citation: reporter citation for a case; empty string for statute/constitution/rule, where 'name' already IS the citation
propositions: what this authority is cited for

case_scotus.name: Rodriguez v. United States
propositions: stop unlawful once prolonged beyond original mission

case_state.name: Simmons v. State
propositions: applies Rodriguez to find a traffic stop unlawfully prolonged

statute.name: AS 28.35.033(e)
propositions: officer must clearly and expressly inform of the right to an independent test

constitution.name: Alaska Const. art. I, § 7
propositions: due process basis for the right

rule.name: Alaska Criminal Rule 5(b)
propositions: implements the right to communicate with counsel or a relative/friend after arrest

authority_schema.why_one_array: Cases, statutes, constitutional provisions, and court rules all serve the same function in a law paragraph — a citation backing a proposition. They only differ in what 'name' and 'citation' look like. One array with a 'type' tag scales to future authority kinds without adding a new array every time one shows up.
authority_schema.why_court_not_jurisdiction: A separate 'jurisdiction' field (federal/state) plus a segment-level 'circuit'/'state' field was the same redundancy the segment-level rewrite fixed. An authority's 'court' value already says everything 'jurisdiction' tried to say, and says it more precisely (AK vs 9th Circuit vs SCOTUS, not just 'state' vs 'federal').
authority_schema.migration_history: citations (case-shaped) -> statutory_citations stopgap -> unified 'authorities' array with a 'jurisdiction' field -> now a single 'court' field, mirroring the same collapse already done at the segment level. All issue files are current as of this note.

court_tagging_convention.SCOTUS: court: 'SCOTUS' — genuine U.S. Supreme Court authority only, including the U.S. Constitution as SCOTUS interprets it. Binding on federal and state courts alike, so it renders in EVERY filing regardless of forum. Do NOT tag a circuit-level case 'SCOTUS' just because you haven't found a split or believe it applies everywhere — if it isn't actually a Supreme Court case, tag it with the real circuit instead.
court_tagging_convention.circuit_specific: court: '9th Circuit' — renders ALONGSIDE the SCOTUS segment (both together, not instead of it), and ONLY for a 'Federal court' filing. Add one whenever you find the 9th Circuit's own case restating, applying, or elaborating a proposition — this is routine, not limited to genuine circuit splits. NEVER rendered for a 'State court' filing, even on the same topic — the 9th Circuit isn't binding on Alaska's state courts, and the working assumption throughout this project has been to rely on binding authority, not persuasive material.
court_tagging_convention.state_specific: court: 'AK' — renders ALONGSIDE the SCOTUS segment (both together), and ONLY for a 'State court' filing. Also used for AK statutes, constitutional provisions, and court rules (see authority_schema) — 'court' means 'whose law this authority represents', not literally 'which court decided it'.
court_tagging_convention.current_scope: Only three court values are in use right now — SCOTUS, 9th Circuit, and AK — matching the one-option dropdowns in case_session_schema.state_name / federal_circuit. Expanding later just means adding a new dropdown option plus a new court value (e.g. 'CA', '2nd Circuit') to the affected issue files — no change to segments, authorities, or the resolver itself.
court_tagging_convention.history: This field was previously split across 'jurisdiction' (federal/state) + 'circuit' (SCOTUS/9th/4th/etc, tagged 'any' before that) + 'state' (AK/CA/etc) on a segment. All three collapsed into this single 'court' field once it became clear a state-court filing should always include SCOTUS by default, which the old three-field split made awkward to express.

steps: 1. desiredCourts = forumToCourts(case_session) — 'State court' -> {SCOTUS, courtCodeForState(case_session.state_name)} e.g. {SCOTUS, AK}; 'Federal court' -> {SCOTUS, case_session.federal_circuit} e.g. {SCOTUS, 9th Circuit}
2. matchingSegments = segments where segment.court IN desiredCourts, status != 'NEEDS_RESEARCH'
3. toRender = matchingSegments, ordered SCOTUS first, then the circuit/state segment
4. IF toRender is empty: set warning (e.g. 'no_authority_for_<court>'), fall back to the SCOTUS segment if one exists — never render nothing, never silently use an unresearched placeholder

5. IF case_session.forum == 'Federal court' AND case_session.federal_circuit NOT IN issue.circuits_reviewed: add soft warning 'circuit_specific_authority_not_researched' — fires even when toRender is non-empty, since it means nobody has checked whether this circuit has its own case worth citing yet, not that none exists. This warning NEVER fires for a 'State court' filing — circuit-specific segments are never pulled into state-court output at all, so there's nothing to flag as unresearched there.
6. text = join segment texts in toRender order; authorities = flattened segment authorities
7. return { text, authorities, warnings: [] }  // warnings is a list — both a step-4 and step-5 warning can fire together

question_types.multiple_choice: answer is a single string, one of the question's options — pick exactly one
question_types.multi_select: answer is an array of strings, a subset of the question's options — pick any number, including zero or all
question_types.short_text: answer is a free-text string, not matched against a fixed option list — used for fact-gathering (e.g. q_duration), not for gating match_condition

condition_shape.description: The shape used by match_condition, and by 'when' inside review_conditions/excluded_explanations, is the same: either a single leaf { question, op, value } or a compound { all: [...] } / { any: [...] } of leaves (and compounds can nest).

ops_for_scalar_answers.description: For yes_no and multiple_choice questions (answer is a single string).

ops_for_array_answers.description: For multi_select questions (answer is an array of strings). Do NOT use equals/in against a multi_select answer — those compare a single value and give unreliable results against an array.

ops.includes: true if the given value (a single option string) is present anywhere in the answer array
ops.not_includes: true if the given value is absent from the answer array
ops.not_empty: true if at least one option was selected, regardless of which — value is omitted for this op
ops.empty: true if no options were selected — value is omitted for this op
